title: Diagnostic laparoscopy for endometriosis
summary: Look, recognise and treat: a 19-year-old with cyclical pelvic pain unresponsive to medical treatment.

steps.title: Plug the diathermy generator into the pendant
steps.hint: Mains lead from the generator into a socket on the ceiling pendant.

steps.title: Where does the patient plate go?
steps.prompt: Where should the return electrode (patient plate) be placed?

choices.text: On a well-perfused muscle mass close to the operation, such as the thigh, on dry hair-free skin
choices.feedback: Correct: a large, well-perfused contact area keeps the current density low.
Poor contact: a burn risk at the plate.
Current concentrates in the metal.
Distance and contact both matter.

steps.title: Apply the patient plate to the thigh
steps.hint: Full, flat contact on the thigh; check the generator's contact alarm clears.

steps.title: Connect the light cable to the laparoscope
steps.hint: Light lead to the scope's light post at the camera port.

steps.title: Connect the camera head
steps.hint: White balance before inserting the scope.

steps.title: Connect the CO2 tubing to the camera port
steps.hint: Insufflation at 12-15 mmHg once the port is in the peritoneal cavity.

steps.title: Why operate?
steps.prompt: Ultrasound of her pelvis was normal. Why is a diagnostic laparoscopy still indicated?

choices.text: Imaging often misses superficial peritoneal endometriosis; only seeing and biopsying lesions confirms it
choices.feedback: Correct: a normal scan does not exclude endometriosis, especially the subtle lesions seen in adolescents.

choices.text: A normal scan rules it out, so this is unnecessary
choices.feedback: Superficial disease is invisible on ultrasound.
Fertility-sparing: the aim is to diagnose and treat lesions.

steps.title: WHO Time Out
steps.prompt: Before skin incision for a diagnostic laparoscopy, the team pauses. What must be confirmed aloud?

choices.text: Patient identity, the procedure, the site and side, and antibiotics given in the last 60 minutes
choices.feedback: Correct: the Time Out confirms who, what and where, and that prophylaxis is in.

choices.text: Only that the consent form is signed
choices.feedback: The signature alone does not prevent wrong-site surgery.

choices.text: Nothing: the site was marked on the ward
choices.feedback: Marking does not replace the Time Out.

steps.hint: The site is the abdomen and pelvis. All three phases of the WHO checklist are mandatory.

steps.title: Positioning
steps.prompt: The patient is anaesthetised. How is she positioned for a pelvic laparoscopy?

choices.text: Lithotomy with the legs supported, arms tucked, ready for head-down (Trendelenburg) tilt once the ports are in
choices.feedback: Correct: head-down tilt lets the bowel fall out of the pelvis so it can be seen.
The pelvis must face the camera.
The bowel would fall into the pelvis and hide it.

steps.hint: Padding at the knees and calves; check the common peroneal nerve is not compressed.

steps.title: Empty the bladder (in-out catheter) before the suprapubic port
steps.hint: A full bladder sits in the path of the lower ports.

steps.title: Pick up the skin preparation
steps.hint: Alcoholic chlorhexidine, applied from the incision site outwards.

steps.title: Prepare the skin over the abdomen
steps.hint: Centre outwards, wider than the incision; let it dry fully before drapes and diathermy (it is flammable).

steps.title: Camera port: umbilicus
steps.hint: Hidden in the navel: the best cosmetic result.

steps.title: Working port: left iliac fossa
steps.hint: Lateral to the rectus sheath, away from the inferior epigastric vessels.

steps.title: Working port: right iliac fossa
steps.hint: Mirror image of the left; inserted under vision.

steps.title: Entry
steps.prompt: How do you enter the abdomen for the camera port in this slim young patient?

choices.text: Open (Hasson) entry at the umbilicus, or Veress at Palmer's point with careful checks
choices.feedback: Correct: in a slim patient the aorta is only a few centimetres below the umbilicus.

choices.text: Blind trocar straight down with force
choices.feedback: The great vessels lie close beneath: a catastrophic injury risk.
The camera port goes in first, then the others under vision.

steps.title: Pneumoperitoneum
steps.prompt: To what pressure do you insufflate CO2?

choices.feedback: Correct: enough room to see, without impairing venous return.
Impairs venous return and ventilation.
No working space.

steps.title: Insert the laparoscope
steps.hint: Warm the lens against fogging; white balance done; look around the entry site first for injury.

steps.title: Survey order
steps.prompt: The scope is in. What do you do first?

choices.text: Inspect the whole abdomen (liver, diaphragm, appendix, bowel), then tilt head-down and survey the pelvis systematically
choices.feedback: Correct: a systematic survey, so nothing is missed and entry injuries are found.
A quick look misses disease and entry injuries.

choices.text: Start treating the first lesion seen
choices.feedback: Map all the disease before treating any of it.

steps.title: The pelvic survey
steps.prompt: Which pelvic sites must be inspected?

choices.text: Uterus, both ovaries and tubes, ovarian fossae, uterosacral ligaments, pouch of Douglas, bladder peritoneum, pelvic side walls, sigmoid and appendix
choices.feedback: Correct: the most common sites are the ovaries, uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas.
Most lesions are on the peritoneum and ovaries.
Peritoneal lesions would be missed.

steps.title: Recognising lesions
steps.prompt: In adolescents, endometriosis often looks like…

choices.text: Subtle clear or red vesicles and flame-like lesions, rather than the classic black 'powder-burn' spots
choices.feedback: Correct: early lesions are subtle; look closely, with the scope near the peritoneum.
Those are typical of older, advanced disease.

choices.text: Nothing visible: it cannot be seen
choices.feedback: It can: it must be looked for carefully.

steps.title: Biopsy a lesion and send it for histology
steps.hint: Histology confirms the diagnosis; label the specimen with its site.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.prompt: A lesion lies on the left pelvic side wall, close to where the ureter runs. How do you treat it?

choices.text: Identify the ureter first, then excise the lesion (lift the peritoneum away) or ablate it with care
choices.feedback: Correct: know where the ureter is before any energy is used on the side wall.
Thermal spread can injure the ureter.
Superficial disease is treated at the same operation where safe.

steps.title: Document
steps.prompt: What do you record before finishing?

choices.text: The site, size and appearance of every lesion and what was done, with photographs, and a stage if used
choices.feedback: Correct: the findings guide follow-up and hormonal treatment.
Too little to guide care.
Record findings now.

steps.title: Release the CO2, remove the ports under vision and close the umbilical fascia
steps.hint: Check each port site for bleeding; let all the gas out to reduce shoulder-tip pain.

steps.title: Close the skin with absorbable subcuticular sutures
steps.hint: They dissolve and need no removal.

steps.title: Going home
steps.prompt: In recovery she asks why her shoulder hurts. What do you tell her?

choices.text: Leftover gas irritates the diaphragm; it settles in 2–3 days and she can go home today
choices.feedback: Correct: referred pain via the phrenic nerve (C3–5); day-case discharge is usual.
It is expected after laparoscopy.

choices.text: She dislocated it on the table
choices.feedback: No.
